Inverse-distance-weighted interpolation, and zonal means

Source: R/spi.R
idwint.Rd

Carries the values of monitors to target points as the mean of the nearest monitors weighted by their distance to the power -p, and averages the targets of each zone. Exposure papers assign monitor readings to places this way: Rahman et al. (2023, sec. 2.3) take "inverse distance squared weighting of observations from up to four nearby (<50 km) monitoring locations" for census tract centroids (p = 2, k = 4, rad = 50, lonlat = TRUE); Wongchanapai et al. (2025) interpolate a surface of annual PM2.5 "using the inverse distance weight method" and take "zonal statistics" per municipality (targets on a grid over the state, zone the municipality of each grid point; they used ArcGIS Pro and state neither the power nor the neighbours, so give both); Wesselbaum (2022) matches each crime "to the measures of the nearest weather, pollution station" (k = 1).

Usage

idwint(
  mx,
  my,
  mv,
  tx,
  ty,
  p = 2,
  k = 0,
  rad = Inf,
  lonlat = FALSE,
  zone = NULL
)

Arguments

mx, my

The coordinates of the monitors.

mv

The value of each monitor (NA allowed).

tx, ty

The coordinates of the targets.

p

The power of the distance, from 0.

k

The number of nearest monitors used, a whole number from 0 (0: all within rad).

rad

The radius: a positive number or Inf.

lonlat

TRUE for longitude and latitude in degrees (distances in kilometres on the sphere); else planar.

zone

NULL or the zone of each target (labels).

Value

Without zone, a data frame, one row per target: val and used, the monitors used. With zone, one row per zone (sorted): zone, val (the zonal mean) and n, the targets with a value.

Details

A target at a monitor's location takes that monitor's value (the mean of the monitors there); else the k nearest monitors within rad (k = 0: all within rad), ties in distance broken by the order of the monitors, weigh d^-p each; p = 0 gives their plain mean. Monitors with a missing value are left out. A target with no monitor within rad is NA. With zone, the zonal mean is the mean of the zone's targets that have a value: with targets on a regular grid, the mean of the interpolated surface over the zone.

References

Rahman, M. M., Lorenzo, M., Ban-Weiss, G., Hasan, Z., Azzouz, M., Eckel, S. P., Conti, D. V., Lurmann, F., Schlaerth, H., Johnston, J., Ko, J., Palinkas, L., Hurlburt, M., Silva, S., Gauderman, W. J., McConnell, R. and Garcia, E. (2023). Ambient temperature and air pollution associations with suicide and homicide mortality in California: a statewide case-crossover study. Science of the Total Environment, 874, 162462. doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2023.162462

Wongchanapai, P., Green, R., Ku, C. S., Peltier, M. R. and Ranjan, S. (2025). Air pollution and intimate partner violence in New Jersey: examining the evidence. Psychology of Violence, 15(6), 682-688. doi:10.1037/vio0000653

Wesselbaum, D. (2022). Violent crimes and homicide in New York City: the role of weather and pollution. Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine, 91, 102430. doi:10.1016/j.jflm.2022.102430

See also

kerexp(), bufexp(), ccross()

Examples

m <- data.frame(x = c(0, 10, 0), y = c(0, 0, 10), pm = c(8, 12, 10))
idwint(m$x, m$y, m$pm, c(5, 0), c(0, 0))
#>   val used
#> 1  10    3
#> 2   8    1
# the nearest monitor only
idwint(m$x, m$y, m$pm, c(9, 1), c(0, 1), k = 1)
#>   val used
#> 1  12    1
#> 2   8    1
# a grid over two zones, and the zonal means
g <- expand.grid(x = 0:10, y = 0:10)
idwint(m$x, m$y, m$pm, g$x, g$y, zone = ifelse(g$x < 5, "west", "east"))
#>   zone      val  n
#> 1 east 10.69539 66
#> 2 west  9.33759 55
